lesson.title: Strings 101: Text as Data
lesson.summary: A string is Python's built-in type for representing text: an ordered sequence of characters created with quotes, which can be joined, compared, and processed like any other value.
lesson.body:
Every program that greets a user by name, reads a file, or prints an error message is working with text, and in Python that text lives in a value of type str, short for string. A string is created simply by surrounding characters with quotes: single quotes like 'hello', double quotes like "hello", or triple quotes like '''hello''' or """hello""" for text that spans multiple lines. Python treats single and double quotes as interchangeable, which is convenient when the text itself contains one kind of quote mark, since you can wrap it in the other kind without extra work, as in "It's a nice day".

What makes strings powerful, and what every later string concept builds on, is that a string is not just a blob of text but an ordered sequence of individual characters. That sequence structure is what will make indexing, slicing, and iteration all possible in the concepts that follow this one; for now, the key idea to internalize is simply that 'PYTHON' is not one indivisible thing, it is six characters sitting in a specific order, and Python keeps track of that order precisely.

Strings can be combined with the + operator, an operation called concatenation, which joins two strings end to end into a new string:

greeting = "Hello"
name = 'Ada'
message = greeting + ", " + name + "!"
print(message)

Trace the concatenation left to right. greeting + ", " produces "Hello, ", then that result plus name produces "Hello, Ada", then that result plus "!" produces "Hello, Ada!". The variable message holds that final combined string, and print(message) outputs Hello, Ada! to the screen. Notice that + only works to join strings to other strings; trying to write "Score: " + 95 raises a TypeError, because 95 is an integer, not a string, and Python will not silently guess what you meant.

Strings also support comparison with ==, which checks whether two strings contain exactly the same characters in exactly the same order and case. "cat" == "cat" is True, but "cat" == "Cat" is False, because uppercase and lowercase letters are considered different characters. This exactness is a common source of bugs for beginners comparing user input, like a typed username, against an expected value, and it is worth remembering once string methods for changing case are introduced later, since normalizing case before comparing is a standard fix.

Every concept that follows in this unit, indexing into a string, slicing out a piece of it, measuring its length, calling built-in methods on it, all treats a string as this same kind of object: an ordered, quoted sequence of characters that can be built with concatenation and compared with equality. Getting comfortable with strings as sequences now is what makes the next several ideas feel like natural extensions rather than new topics. Even an empty string, written as "" with nothing between the quotes, still counts as a valid string containing zero characters, and it will matter later once you start measuring and looping over strings whose exact contents are not known in advance.
